title: Giving wisely
tomorrow: the Japji says takers grow tired of taking. why would anyone?

lines: A THUMB OVER A DONATE BUTTON.
cards: Simran's thumb is hovering over a donate button. The video is heartbreaking: slow piano, a family in tears, a total climbing fast while she watches.

Her daswandh envelope, money from her weekend dispatch shifts, sits on the desk next to her. Bebe Jaswant walks past with a bowl of green chilies from the garden, reads the screen over her shoulder, and asks one question.
Who gets it? Simran opens her mouth to answer. And realizes she has no idea.

teach.b: Sikhs have asked Bebe's question before.
Tradition says that in the Gurus' time, offerings from faraway sangats were gathered by appointed collectors, the masands, and carried to the Guru, for langar and the community's needs.

teach.h: SOME GREW GREEDY; THE GURU ENDED IT.
teach.b: Over time, tradition says, some masands grew greedy: they kept what they collected and lorded it over the people who gave. Guru Gobind Singh ended the system and asked Sikhs to bring their offerings to the Guru directly.
Here's the part to tell a friend tonight. The giving was never the problem. The middle was.
So giving wisely isn't suspicion of everyone who asks.
It's three plain questions. Who is this for? Who handles it on the way?
What does it actually do when it lands?

teach.h: ANG 1245: GIVE WITH YOUR OWN HAND.
teach.b: On ang 1245, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it with their own hand recognizes the path. With their own hand.
That evening Simran closes the video. She asks Bebe who runs the food pantry shelf at the gurdwara, and on Sunday she carries the envelope there herself.
A volunteer shows her the shelves: rice, lentils, diapers, a list of families. She can see exactly where it lands.

how: Many gurdwaras take daswandh and other offerings for langar and community needs, and some Sikhs research a cause or give directly where they can see the help land.

o: giving only to people you already know well
giving where it truly helps, and asking who gets it
giving the smallest amount that still counts

p: earn honestly, give with your own hand

s: the more moving the appeal, the more good the money does
the story of the masands says the middle matters: who handles it and what it does.
tradition says Guru Gobind Singh ended the masand system and asked Sikhs to give directly
the giving was never the problem; the middle was.
giving wisely means trusting no one who asks
it's three plain questions: who is it for, who handles it, what does it do.

games.q: you have a little set aside to give. a viral appeal is everywhere today; the gurdwara's pantry shelf is half empty. what does today's story say to do first?
o: ask who gets it, who handles it, and what it does, then give.
give to whichever appeal moves you most, as fast as you can.
keep it until you're sure every cause is perfectly honest.
games.why: after the masands, the Guru asked Sikhs to bring offerings directly. Simran carried hers to the pantry shelf and saw where it landed.

practice: Bring to mind one cause you'd like your share to reach. Name what you hope it does, then the one thing you don't yet know about it, then one simple way you could find out.
Then set the plan down and let your hands rest open in your lap for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Giving wisely. Giving where it truly helps, and knowing who carries it there.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: masand, the collectors who carried the sangats' offerings to the Guru.

carryVoice: The open hand stays open, and it also asks who gets it: give wisely. See you tomorrow.
